course.title: Java
course.description: Build Java foundations, then grow toward advanced algorithms.

units.title: Foundations
units.description: Name values, make decisions, and repeat steps.

lessons.title: Variables
lessons.concept: A Java variable has a type and a name. Use = to assign a value; an ordinary variable can be reassigned.

questions.prompt: Which declaration stores a whole number?
questions.explanation: int is Java's usual 32-bit whole-number type.

questions.prompt: Complete the assignment operator.
questions.explanation: A single = assigns a value to a variable.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: score stores 4, which println displays.

questions.prompt: Inside main, create score, increase it, then print it.
questions.explanation: Declare score before using it; print after the update.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: backup holds its own copy of the integer value 2.

lessons.title: Value Types
lessons.concept: Java uses declared types. int stores whole numbers, double stores decimals, boolean stores true or false, and String stores text.

questions.prompt: Which type stores true or false?
questions.explanation: boolean has exactly two values: true and false.

questions.prompt: Complete the type for decimal values.
questions.explanation: A decimal literal such as 3.5 is a double by default.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: Java prints a boolean using lowercase true or false.

questions.prompt: Inside main, create numeric text, parse it, then print the integer.
questions.explanation: parseInt converts the numeric text before number is printed.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: Parsing creates integer 4, so numeric addition gives 6.

lessons.title: Operators
lessons.concept: Arithmetic uses +, -, *, / and %. Dividing two ints discards the fractional part; % gives the remainder.

questions.prompt: Which operator multiplies two numbers?
questions.explanation: Java uses * for multiplication.

questions.prompt: Complete the expression to get the remainder.
questions.explanation: % gives the remainder after division.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: Both operands are ints, so the fractional part is discarded.

questions.prompt: Inside main, create price, calculate total, then print it.
questions.explanation: Calculate total after declaring price; print the result last.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: Multiplication has higher precedence than addition.

lessons.title: Conditionals
lessons.concept: if checks a boolean condition in parentheses. Braces group statements; else if checks another case and else handles the remaining case.

questions.prompt: Which keyword starts a conditional?
questions.explanation: if runs a statement or block when its boolean condition is true.

questions.prompt: Complete the comparison for equal numbers.
questions.explanation: == compares numeric values; = assigns a value.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: 3 is below 5, so the else block runs.

questions.prompt: Inside main, declare ready, test it, then finish the block.
questions.explanation: Declare ready before its condition; the print belongs inside the braces.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: The first condition fails; the second condition matches score 8.

lessons.title: For Loops
lessons.concept: A for loop combines an initialization, a condition and an update. Its body repeats while the condition is true.

questions.prompt: In i++, what happens to i?
questions.explanation: i++ increments the integer by one.

questions.prompt: Complete the condition to visit 0, 1 and 2.
questions.explanation: i < 3 excludes 3, so the body runs three times.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: The loop adds 0, 1, and 2.

questions.prompt: Inside main, initialize count, run the loop, then print count.
questions.explanation: Initialize the counter before the loop; print after all iterations.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: The loop visits 1, 3, and 5, whose sum is 9.

units.title: Methods & Collections
units.description: Reuse code and organize values into useful structures.

lessons.title: Methods
lessons.concept: A method groups reusable statements. A parameter receives input and return sends back a value. These examples use static methods called from main.

questions.prompt: What does return do in a value-returning method?
options: Sends a result to the caller
questions.explanation: return ends the method and supplies its result to the caller.

questions.prompt: Complete the return type for an integer result.
questions.explanation: The method returns a whole number, so its return type is int.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: The parameter receives 4 and the method returns 4 × 2.

questions.prompt: Order this complete method to add one to n.
questions.explanation: A method starts with its signature, then its body, then the closing brace.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: The inner call returns 4; the outer call returns 5.

lessons.title: Strings
lessons.concept: String holds text. For the ASCII text here, length() counts characters and charAt uses indexes starting at 0. equals compares text content.

questions.prompt: Which method counts characters in word?
questions.explanation: String.length() returns the character count for this ASCII text.

questions.prompt: Complete the method to compare text content.
questions.explanation: equals compares String contents; == compares object references.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: Index 1 selects the second character, o.

questions.prompt: Inside main, create word, make uppercase text, then print it.
questions.explanation: toUpperCase creates uppercase text before it is printed.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: substring includes index 1 and excludes index 4.

lessons.title: Arrays
lessons.concept: An array stores a fixed number of values of one type. Indexes start at 0; the length field gives the number of slots.

questions.prompt: Which declaration creates an int array?
questions.explanation: int[] declares an array of integers.

questions.prompt: Complete the field to count array slots.
questions.explanation: Arrays use the length field, without parentheses.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: Index 1 selects the second array element.

questions.prompt: Inside main, create the array, update its first item, then print it.
questions.explanation: The array must exist before its first element is updated.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: The first item is now 9; the last item remains 6.

lessons.title: Hash Maps
lessons.concept: HashMap stores key-value pairs. put adds or replaces a value; get reads it, and getOrDefault supplies a fallback for an absent key.

questions.prompt: What does a HashMap connect?
questions.explanation: Each unique key maps to one associated value.

questions.prompt: Complete the method to store Mina's score.
questions.explanation: put stores or replaces the value for a key.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: Kai is absent, so the fallback 0 is returned.

questions.prompt: Inside main, create the map, store Mina's score, then read it.
questions.explanation: Create the map before inserting a pair; read it after insertion.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: Replacing Mina does not add a key; Kai creates the second key.

lessons.title: Classes & Objects
lessons.concept: A class defines an object's fields and behavior. new creates an instance; a constructor sets its initial state.

questions.prompt: Which keyword creates a class instance?
questions.explanation: new allocates an instance and invokes its constructor.

questions.prompt: Complete the field assignment in the constructor.
questions.explanation: The constructor assigns start to the instance field value.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: The constructor stores its argument 4 in value.

questions.prompt: Inside main, create a Counter, update its field, then print it. Counter has an int value field.
questions.explanation: Create the object before accessing its field; print after updating it.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: The two new expressions create separate objects with independent fields.

units.title: Complexity & Search
units.description: Bound growth, find values, and maintain shrinking search spaces.

lessons.title: Big O
lessons.concept: Big O describes an upper bound on growth as input size increases. Ignore fixed factors, but count dependent loops carefully: two separate linear scans stay linear; two full nested scans are quadratic. These lessons use the usual RAM model with constant-time arithmetic on small integers. Java examples belong inside main; import java.util.*. Local helper classes are shown where needed.

questions.prompt: What does O(n) describe?
options: An algorithm that always beats O(log n)
An upper bound proportional to input size
questions.explanation: Big O measures growth, not exact running time.

questions.prompt: Visit every valid array index exactly once, from first to last.
questions.code: for (int i = 0; i ___ values.length; i++) { /* visit */ }
questions.explanation: The last valid index is length minus one.

questions.prompt: Trace the code. What is the output?
questions.explanation: Each of three outer iterations performs three inner increments.

questions.prompt: Initialize the empty input and counter, perform the scan, then print 0.
questions.explanation: An empty collection skips the loop and leaves count zero.

questions.prompt: One n-element scan is followed by a separate n-element scan. What is the tight growth bound?
questions.explanation: Adding two linear costs remains linear.

lessons.title: Linear Search
lessons.concept: Linear search inspects elements in order and works without sorting. Return the first matching index, or a sentinel such as -1 when no match exists. Before each step, every earlier element has already been ruled out. Worst-case work grows with the collection size. Java examples belong inside main; import java.util.*. Local helper classes are shown where needed.

questions.prompt: Which input can linear search handle directly?
questions.explanation: Linear search needs no ordering assumption.

questions.prompt: Complete the condition that identifies a matching element.
questions.code: if (values[i] ___ target) { return i; }
questions.explanation: Equality identifies the target; earlier indices have already been checked.

questions.prompt: Trace the code. What is the output?
questions.explanation: The first 6 is at zero-based index 2.

questions.prompt: Initialize an empty search with -1, scan for 9, then print the not-found result.
questions.explanation: No element is visited, so the not-found sentinel survives.

questions.prompt: The target is absent from n elements. How many equality checks does this linear search need?
questions.explanation: An absent target requires inspecting every element.

lessons.title: Binary Search
lessons.concept: Binary search repeatedly halves an ordered candidate interval. In an ascending array, compare the middle value and discard the half that cannot contain the target. This lesson uses inclusive bounds [left, right]; moving past mid guarantees progress. Sorting first has its own cost. Java examples belong inside main; import java.util.*. Local helper classes are shown where needed.

questions.prompt: What must hold for ordinary binary search on an array?
options: The array is sorted in the comparison order
questions.explanation: Ordering lets one comparison eliminate an entire half.

questions.prompt: With inclusive bounds, keep searching while at least one candidate remains.
questions.code: while (left ___ right) { /* inspect middle */ }
questions.explanation: left equal to right still represents one unchecked element.

questions.prompt: Trace the code. What is the output?
questions.explanation: After discarding values below 7, the algorithm finds index 3.

questions.prompt: Order the one-candidate boundary check so it prints 0.
questions.explanation: The inclusive loop condition preserves the singleton candidate.

questions.prompt: For one lookup in an unsorted array, what is the cost of comparison-sorting before binary search?
options: Sorting is unnecessary for binary search
questions.explanation: The sorting cost dominates the subsequent logarithmic lookup.

lessons.title: Two Pointers
lessons.concept: For pair sums in an ascending array, start at both ends. A sum below the target means the left value is too small for any remaining partner at or below right; move left forward. A sum above the target moves right backward. Keep left < right to avoid using one element twice. Java examples belong inside main; import java.util.*. Local helper classes are shown where needed.

questions.prompt: Which input supports the opposite-end pair-sum technique directly?
questions.explanation: Sorted values justify discarding candidates after each comparison.

questions.prompt: A pair sum is too small. Move the left pointer toward larger values.
questions.code: left ___ 1;
questions.explanation: Increasing left raises its value in an ascending array.

questions.prompt: Trace the code. What is the output?
questions.explanation: The first sum is 9; moving left finds 2 + 8.

questions.prompt: Order the guard that rejects using the sole element twice.
blocks: boolean found = left < right && a[left] + a[right] == 10;
answer: boolean found = left < right && a[left] + a[right] == 10;
questions.explanation: Distinct indices require left strictly less than right.

questions.prompt: In an already sorted n-element array, why does the pair-sum scan take O(n) time?
options: The sum operation sorts the array
Each move shrinks the interval by one
Both pointers restart after every comparison
questions.explanation: Each pointer moves in one direction, and the interval only shrinks.

lessons.title: Sliding Window
lessons.concept: A fixed-size sliding window reuses a running aggregate across adjacent subarrays. For a window of k values, subtract the outgoing value and add the incoming value. Initialize from a real window so all-negative inputs work. Require 1 <= k <= n. Variable windows need additional monotonicity assumptions. Java examples belong inside main; import java.util.*. Local helper classes are shown where needed.

questions.prompt: What does a fixed-size sliding window avoid?
options: Recomputing every overlapping sum from scratch
questions.explanation: Adjacent windows share all but two values.

questions.prompt: Remove the outgoing value before adding the incoming value.
questions.code: sum = sum ___ outgoing + incoming;
questions.explanation: Subtracting outgoing preserves exactly the current window sum.

questions.prompt: Trace the code. What is the output?
questions.explanation: The two-element sums are 3, 6, and 6.

questions.prompt: Order initialization for an all-negative length-two window; print -5.
questions.explanation: Initializing best to zero would invent a nonexistent window.

questions.prompt: Why can the usual shrink-when-sum-exceeds-target window fail when negative values are allowed?
options: Removing a negative value can increase the sum
Every window must have length one
questions.explanation: Negative values break the monotonicity that justifies that shrinking rule.

units.title: Data Structures
units.description: Choose and reason about stacks, queues, links, trees, and key lookup.

lessons.title: Stacks
lessons.concept: A stack removes the newest item first: last in, first out. Push and pop at the same end. This matches nested parentheses, undo history, and explicit DFS worklists. Check for an empty stack before accessing its top. Dynamic-array stacks usually offer amortized constant-time push, not a guarantee for every resizing operation. Java examples belong inside main; import java.util.*. Local helper classes are shown where needed.

questions.prompt: Which item does a stack remove first?
questions.explanation: Stacks follow last in, first out.

questions.prompt: Complete the operation that removes the top stack item.
questions.code: int value = stack.___();
questions.explanation: Pop removes the most recently added stack item.

questions.prompt: Trace the code. What is the output?
questions.explanation: Removing 3 exposes 2 as the new top.

questions.prompt: Order a safe empty-stack read; print -1 instead of popping.
questions.explanation: The emptiness guard prevents invalid top access.

questions.prompt: While validating parentheses, a closing bracket arrives with an empty stack. What should happen?
options: Push the closing bracket as a valid opener
Reject immediately: it has no opening partner
questions.explanation: A closing bracket cannot match an opening bracket that never appeared.

lessons.title: Queues
lessons.concept: A queue serves the oldest item first: first in, first out. Use a deque, circular buffer, or an array with a moving head index. In JavaScript, repeated Array.shift() may move remaining items, so do not assume it is constant time. A growing head-index array also needs eventual compaction or bounded-buffer management to reclaim consumed storage. Java examples belong inside main; import java.util.*. Local helper classes are shown where needed.

questions.prompt: Which item leaves a FIFO queue first?
options: The item with the shortest name
questions.explanation: FIFO preserves arrival order.

questions.prompt: Read the next FIFO item using the intended queue operation.
questions.code: int value = queue.___();
questions.explanation: Advance the head or remove from the front to preserve FIFO order.

questions.prompt: Trace the code. What is the output?
questions.explanation: After removing 4, the oldest remaining item is 7.

questions.prompt: Order a safe empty-queue read that prints -1.
questions.explanation: Check for queued items before accessing the front.

questions.prompt: Why use ArrayDeque.removeFirst() instead of ArrayList.remove(0) for a FIFO graph-traversal queue?
options: It eliminates the need for visited state
It avoids shifting the remaining array elements
It makes every graph traversal O(1)
questions.explanation: ArrayDeque front removal is amortized O(1); ArrayList.remove(0) shifts elements and takes O(n).

lessons.title: Linked Lists
lessons.concept: A singly linked list stores each value with a link to its successor. To remove a node when its predecessor is known, redirect the predecessor link. Searching for that predecessor can still take linear time. Reversal must save the next link before overwriting it, and every traversal must account for an empty head. Java examples belong inside main; import java.util.*. Local helper classes are shown where needed.

questions.prompt: What connects adjacent nodes in a singly linked list?
questions.explanation: Each node stores a link to its successor.

questions.prompt: Skip the node after current without losing the remaining chain.
questions.code: current.next = current.next.___;
questions.explanation: Linking to the successor’s successor bypasses exactly one node.

questions.prompt: Trace the code. What is the output?
questions.explanation: Redirecting the first link bypasses the node containing 2.

questions.prompt: Save the next link, then rewire the one node, then print its value. Initialize the node first.
blocks:
class Node { int value = 4; Node next; }
Node current = new Node(), previous = null;
answer:
class Node { int value = 4; Node next; }
Node current = new Node(), previous = null;
questions.explanation: Saving next first preserves access to the unprocessed chain.

questions.prompt: What is the worst-case time to find and delete a value in a singly linked list of n nodes?
options: O(n), because finding the node may scan the list
O(1), because every deletion is constant time
questions.explanation: Known-predecessor rewiring is constant time; finding that predecessor may be linear.

lessons.title: Binary Trees
lessons.concept: A binary tree gives each node up to two children. Define height here as the number of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path, with an empty tree having height zero. A binary search tree adds an ordering invariant, but it is not automatically balanced. Shape determines whether search is logarithmic or linear. Java examples belong inside main; import java.util.*. Local helper classes are shown where needed.

questions.prompt: How many children can a binary-tree node have?
questions.explanation: A binary tree permits zero, one, or two children per node.

questions.prompt: An empty subtree has height zero. Add one for the current node.
questions.code: return ___ + Math.max(height(node.left), height(node.right));
questions.explanation: The current node contributes one to the longer child path.

questions.prompt: Trace the code. What is the output?
questions.explanation: There are three nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path.

questions.prompt: Order the empty-tree base case before its height is used.
questions.explanation: The null base case stops recursion before any child access.

questions.prompt: Insert sorted distinct keys into an ordinary unbalanced BST. What can happen to search time?
options: It becomes O(n) as the tree degenerates into a chain
It stays O(log n) for every insertion order
It becomes O(1) because keys are sorted
The tree automatically becomes a heap
questions.explanation: A BST ordering invariant alone does not guarantee balanced height.

lessons.title: Hash Maps
lessons.concept: A hash table maps keys to buckets using a hash function. Good distribution and controlled load support expected constant-time basic operations; collisions, resizing, and adversarial inputs prevent a blanket worst-case O(1) claim. JavaScript Map promises average sublinear access rather than a specific implementation. Distinguish a missing key from a stored zero. Java examples belong inside main; import java.util.*. Local helper classes are shown where needed.

questions.prompt: What is a collision in a hash table?
options: Different keys map to the same bucket
Two keys must have equal values
questions.explanation: Collisions require a strategy to keep distinct keys distinguishable.

questions.prompt: Treat a missing frequency as zero before adding one.
questions.code: counts.put(value, counts.getOrDefault(value, ___) + 1);
questions.explanation: A first occurrence must produce a count of one.

questions.prompt: Trace the code. What is the output?
questions.explanation: The key 2 occurs twice.

questions.prompt: Order a missing-key read that prints zero without raising an error.
questions.explanation: An explicit default handles absence without assuming the key exists.

questions.prompt: A hash table uses linear collision chains. If all n keys share one bucket, how long can lookup take?
options: O(log n) without changing the chains
O(n²) for a single chain scan
questions.explanation: Expected constant-time lookup depends on hash distribution; one long chain can require linear work.

units.title: Algorithms
units.description: Combine sorting, graph traversal, priority structures, and justified greedy choices.

lessons.title: Merge Sort
lessons.concept: Merge sort divides an array, sorts each half, and merges ordered runs. The merge invariant keeps the output sorted while both pointers mark the smallest unused value in each run. Taking the left item on equal keys preserves stability. Standard array merge sort uses O(n log n) time and O(n) auxiliary storage. Java examples belong inside main; import java.util.*. Local helper classes are shown where needed.

questions.prompt: Which operation combines merge sort’s recursively sorted halves?
options: Merging the smallest remaining front values
questions.explanation: Comparing the run fronts preserves sorted output.

questions.prompt: To keep equal keys in original order, choose the left run on ties.
questions.code: if (left[i] ___ right[j]) { /* take left[i] */ }
questions.explanation: Left-first ties preserve the original order of equal keys.

questions.prompt: Trace the code. What is the output?
questions.explanation: The merge repeatedly takes the smallest unused run front.

questions.prompt: The right run is empty. Order the remaining-left copy to print 4,8.
questions.explanation: When one run ends, copy the other run’s remaining values.

questions.prompt: There are log₂ n merge levels with O(n) total work per level. What follows?
questions.explanation: Multiply the number of levels by the work per level.

lessons.title: Breadth-First Search
lessons.concept: BFS explores a graph in distance layers using a FIFO queue. Mark a vertex when enqueuing it so cycles do not repeatedly schedule the same vertex. In an unweighted graph, first discovery gives the minimum number of edges from the source. With adjacency lists and efficient queues, time is O(V + E). Java examples belong inside main; import java.util.*. Local helper classes are shown where needed.

questions.prompt: Which worklist makes BFS explore distance layers?
options: An unsorted set with arbitrary removal
questions.explanation: FIFO processes earlier discoveries before the next layer.

questions.prompt: Set an unseen neighbor’s distance when it enters the queue.
questions.code: distance[v] = distance[u] + ___;
questions.explanation: Traversing one unweighted edge adds one to the distance.

questions.prompt: Trace the code. What is the output?
questions.explanation: Vertex 3 is reached through 1 or 2 in two edges.

questions.prompt: Order discovery of a source with a self-loop: mark it before enqueuing.
questions.explanation: Marking on discovery prevents the self-loop from adding the source again.

questions.prompt: Edges have different positive weights. Does ordinary BFS guarantee the smallest total weight?
options: Only if vertices are numbered consecutively
No; its layers minimize edge count, not arbitrary weight
Yes, if the source has two neighbors
questions.explanation: Use an appropriate weighted shortest-path algorithm when edge costs differ.

lessons.title: Depth-First Search
lessons.concept: DFS follows one branch before backtracking. Use recursion or an explicit stack, and mark vertices before exploring their neighbors. Neighbor order determines a particular traversal order. On a graph with cycles, visited state is essential. Deep recursion may exceed the language’s call-stack limits even when the algorithm is correct. Java examples belong inside main; import java.util.*. Local helper classes are shown where needed.

questions.prompt: What characterizes depth-first search?
options: Always choose the smallest edge weight
Always visit the nearest layer first
questions.explanation: DFS postpones siblings while it explores the current branch.

questions.prompt: Mark a vertex before recursive calls to prevent cycling back into it.
questions.code: seen.___(u);
questions.explanation: Early marking stops back edges from starting duplicate traversals.

questions.prompt: Trace the code. What is the output?
questions.explanation: DFS explores 1 and its child 3 before returning to 2.

questions.prompt: Initialize the empty graph and stack, apply the source-exists guard, then print the stack size.
blocks:
int[][] graph = {};
Deque<Integer> pending = new ArrayDeque<>();
answer:
int[][] graph = {};
Deque<Integer> pending = new ArrayDeque<>();
questions.explanation: An empty graph has no source vertex to schedule.

questions.prompt: To detect cycles in a directed graph, why distinguish active recursion-stack vertices from finished vertices?
options: An edge to an active vertex proves a directed cycle
Every edge to any visited vertex proves a directed cycle
Finished vertices cannot have outgoing edges
questions.explanation: An active vertex is an ancestor on the current path; a finished vertex need not be.

lessons.title: Binary Heaps
lessons.concept: A binary min-heap keeps each parent no greater than its children. The root is the minimum, but the entire array is not sorted. Inserting or removing the root usually needs O(log n) repair; peek is O(1). Building a heap bottom-up is O(n). Standard C++ priority_queue is a max-heap unless its comparator is changed. Java examples belong inside main; import java.util.*. Local helper classes are shown where needed.
examples:
PriorityQueue<Integer> heap = new PriorityQueue<>(List.of(7, 2, 5));
System.out.println(heap.peek());

questions.prompt: Which property defines a min-heap?
options: Every parent is no greater than its children
Every child is smaller than its parent
questions.explanation: The local parent-child rule places a minimum at the root.

questions.prompt: For zero-based heap indexing, find the left child of index i.
questions.code: int left = 2 * i + ___;
questions.explanation: Zero-based children are at indices 2i + 1 and 2i + 2.

questions.prompt: Trace the code. What is the output?
questions.code:
PriorityQueue<Integer> heap = new PriorityQueue<>(List.of(7, 2, 5));
System.out.println(heap.peek());
questions.explanation: The min-heap root contains the smallest inserted value.

questions.prompt: Order a safe read of an empty min-heap; print -1.
questions.explanation: Peek is only valid after confirming the heap has an item.

questions.prompt: Maintain the largest k values in a min-heap while scanning n values, with 1 <= k <= n. What is the standard time bound?
questions.explanation: Each candidate needs at most one logarithmic heap update on at most k entries.

lessons.title: Greedy Algorithms
lessons.concept: Greedy algorithms commit to a locally preferred choice. They need a correctness argument, such as an exchange argument, rather than intuition alone. For maximizing the number of non-overlapping nonempty half-open intervals [start, end), with start < end, choosing earliest finish time is safe. Greedy largest-coin change is not optimal for arbitrary denominations. Java examples belong inside main; import java.util.*. Local helper classes are shown where needed.

questions.prompt: What must justify a greedy choice?
options: A proof that the choice preserves some optimal solution
The choice looks attractive on one example
The choice uses the largest number
The input has fewer than ten elements
questions.explanation: A local preference is safe only when a correctness argument supports it.

questions.prompt: Half-open intervals may touch endpoints. Accept the next interval if it starts after or at the previous end.
questions.code: if (start ___ lastEnd) { /* accept */ }
questions.explanation: Half-open intervals ending and starting at the same point do not overlap.

questions.prompt: Trace the code. What is the output?
questions.explanation: Earliest-finish selection accepts [1,2) and then [2,4).

questions.prompt: Order a largest-coin greedy trace for coins 4,3,1 and amount 6; it uses three coins.
questions.explanation: Greedy takes 4 + 1 + 1; the optimal solution is 3 + 3.

questions.prompt: Coins are 1, 3, and 4; the amount is 6. What defeats largest-coin-first greedy?
questions.explanation: This counterexample shows arbitrary coin systems need a different algorithm.

units.title: Expert DSA
units.description: Reason about DP dependencies, weighted paths, connectivity, and shared prefixes.

lessons.title: Memoization
lessons.concept: Memoization caches results of overlapping subproblems in a top-down recurrence. The cache key must include every input that affects the result. Store results before returning, and distinguish absence from a cached zero. For the recurrence ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2), with ways(0)=ways(1)=1, caching reduces repeated work to O(n) states. Java examples belong inside main; import java.util.*. Local helper classes are shown where needed.

questions.prompt: What does memoization reuse?
options: Any result with a similar-looking name
The result of a previously solved identical state
questions.explanation: Identical subproblems can share their computed result.

questions.prompt: A zero result is valid. Test cache membership rather than truthiness.
questions.code: if (memo.___(key)) return memo.get(key);
questions.explanation: Membership checks preserve valid cached results such as zero.

questions.prompt: Trace the code. What is the output?
questions.explanation: The cached recurrence produces 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8.

questions.prompt: Order a cache read that recognizes zero as an existing result.
questions.explanation: A cached zero is a computed answer, not a missing state.

questions.prompt: A path-count function depends on both vertex and remaining steps. What must its memoization key include?
options: Neither; one global cached result is enough
questions.explanation: Different remaining budgets at the same vertex can have different answers.

lessons.title: Tabulation & 0/1 Knapsack
lessons.concept: Tabulation fills a DP table in dependency order. In one-dimensional 0/1 knapsack, dp[c] stores the best value within capacity c using processed items. Traverse capacities downward for each item so dp[c-weight] still excludes that item. Forward traversal would allow reusing the same item. These examples use nonnegative values and positive integer weights. Java examples belong inside main; import java.util.*. Local helper classes are shown where needed.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes tabulation from recursive memoization?
options: It requires every state to be independent
It fills states iteratively in dependency order
questions.explanation: Tabulation explicitly schedules state evaluation instead of relying on recursive calls.

questions.prompt: Process capacities downward so each 0/1 item is used at most once.
questions.code: for (int c = capacity; c >= weight; c___) { /* update dp[c] */ }
questions.explanation: Descending capacities prevent reading a state already updated by the current item.

questions.prompt: Trace the code. What is the output?
questions.explanation: Only one weight-2 item exists, so capacity 4 still yields value 3.

questions.prompt: Order the zero-capacity base case. It must remain 0.
questions.explanation: With positive item weights, zero capacity cannot hold any item.

questions.prompt: Why is O(nW) knapsack DP called pseudo-polynomial when weights and capacity are binary-encoded?
options: W can be exponential in the number of bits used to encode it
nW is always exponential in n
All table entries are floating-point numbers
The algorithm cannot return exact values
questions.explanation: Running time depends on the numeric capacity, not merely its encoded bit length.

lessons.title: Dijkstra’s Algorithm
lessons.concept: Dijkstra solves single-source shortest paths when every edge weight is nonnegative. Finalize the unvisited vertex with the smallest tentative distance, then relax its outgoing edges. Negative edges invalidate the finalization argument. The tiny examples use a dense O(V²) implementation; a suitable indexed binary heap gives O((V + E) log V). Infinity denotes an unreachable vertex. Java examples belong inside main; import java.util.*. Local helper classes are shown where needed.

questions.prompt: Which condition supports Dijkstra’s usual finalization proof?
options: The graph must be a tree
questions.explanation: Nonnegative edges prevent a later detour from improving a finalized distance.

questions.prompt: Relax an edge only when the candidate distance improves the current best.
questions.code: if (dist[u] + weight ___ dist[v]) { dist[v] = dist[u] + weight; }
questions.explanation: Relaxation keeps the smallest discovered distance to each vertex.

questions.prompt: Trace the code. What is the output?
questions.explanation: The path 0 → 2 → 1 costs 1 + 2, improving the direct cost 4.

questions.prompt: Order an unreachable-distance guard so no infinity is mistaken for a finite path.
questions.explanation: An untouched infinite distance means the vertex is unreachable.

questions.prompt: Edges are S→A=2, S→B=5, B→A=-4. Why can finalizing A at 2 fail?
options: Dijkstra requires all edge weights to equal 1
There must be a negative cycle
The later path through B has cost 1
questions.explanation: A negative edge can improve a distance after its vertex was finalized.

lessons.title: Disjoint Sets
lessons.concept: Disjoint-set union maintains components using parent forests. Find follows parent links to a representative; union links representatives, not arbitrary interior nodes. Path compression shortens find paths. Combining compression with union by rank or size gives amortized O(α(n)) operations, not a universal worst-case O(1) guarantee. DSU supports merging connectivity, but ordinary DSU does not support arbitrary edge deletions. Java examples belong inside main; import java.util.*. Local helper classes are shown where needed.

questions.prompt: What does find(x) return in a disjoint-set forest?
questions.explanation: Following parent links reaches the component’s representative root.

questions.prompt: Compress a path by storing the representative returned by recursive find.
questions.code: parent[x] = ___(parent[x]);
questions.explanation: The assignment redirects x straight to its representative.

questions.prompt: Trace the code. What is the output?
questions.explanation: Full path compression rewrites parent[3] to the root 0.

questions.prompt: Initialize the forest and component count, apply the same-component union guard, then print the unchanged count 1.
blocks: int rootA = parent[0], rootB = parent[1], components = 1;
answer: int rootA = parent[0], rootB = parent[1], components = 1;
questions.explanation: Union changes the component count only when the representatives differ.

questions.prompt: Which combination gives DSU its amortized O(α(n)) operation bound?
options: Only checking whether indices are equal
Sorting the parent array after each find
Path compression plus union by rank or size
questions.explanation: The near-constant amortized bound relies on both forest-balancing and path-compression heuristics.

lessons.title: Tries & Prefix Search
lessons.concept: A trie shares character paths among words with common prefixes. A terminal flag distinguishes a complete word from a mere prefix. Searching a word of length L takes O(L) when each child lookup is constant time, for example a fixed alphabet array; map-backed child lookup depends on the map. Deleting a word must preserve branches and terminal flags needed by other words. Java examples belong inside main; import java.util.*. Local helper classes are shown where needed.

questions.prompt: What does a trie path naturally represent?
options: A sorted list of all stored values
A shortest path through a weighted graph
A sequence of characters forming a prefix
questions.explanation: Words with common prefixes share their initial character path.

questions.prompt: After following every character, exact-word search must check the terminal flag.
questions.code: return node.___;
questions.explanation: A path can exist without marking the end of a stored word.

questions.prompt: Trace the code. What is the output?
questions.explanation: The shared prefix ca branches to t and r.

blocks:

questions.explanation: An empty word ends at the root without traversing any character.

questions.prompt: A trie contains car and cart. To delete car while preserving cart, what is essential?
options: Clear car’s terminal flag but keep the branch to t
Delete every node shared by both words
questions.explanation: A shared prefix remains necessary for the longer stored word.
